I went to rehab for alcoholism. In my case, a series of events led to drinking more casually, but only socially. Then it was every day, then every day but at home, and eventually, it became an addiction. In treatment, they taught the AA 12 step program. The AA doctrine says that you are powerless over your addiction. I had a big problem with this because to me, that was saying you were not required to take personal responsibility. That mind set was apparent in many. I rejected the notion that I was powerless. I took responsibility for my actions, completed in-patient treatment, and I've been sober ever since.

I still went to AA meetings for about 6 months. It was a good support system. I then transitioned to the strong support system I have with my family, and have had no problems. I drink maybe twice a year, for my anniversary and my wife's birthday, but never in excess. It has not led me to want to drink more, and I loathe being around people that are drunk.

I say all this to offer an explanation, that a large portion (but certainly not all in my own experiences) of alcoholics have the mind set that they are powerless, and therefore, not responsible for their actions. This gives them license to behave as if they're special, that no one could possibly understand them, and many have trouble managing their anger. I have seen all of this first hand.

I wouldn't say it's more socially acceptable. There are many spin offs of AA, everything from Narcotics Anonymous, to more targeted ones like Cocaine Anonymous. They all share the same basic principles of AA, that they're powerless over their addiction. The strange thing, and perhaps contradictory to my point, is that the shoulder-on-chip syndrome that you reference, seems to be unique to AA and their followers.
